name: Lomekwian
date_note: c. 3.3 million years ago; single site complex (Lomekwi 3, West Turkana)
making_significance: The oldest known knapped stone tools, made before the genus Homo is securely attested.
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society. Single-site evidence; some researchers question the dating and context.

name: Oldowan
date_note: c. 2.6 million to c. 1 million years ago (persists alongside Acheulean)
making_significance: Simple flaked cores and sharp flakes made by early hominins for butchery and plant processing.
defined_by: Louis and Mary Leakey, after Olduvai Gorge (Tanzania)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0)
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society. Also at Dmanisi (Georgia).

name: Acheulean
date_note: c. 1.76 million to c. 130,000 years ago; varies by region
making_significance: Hominins shaped symmetrical handaxes, a sign of planned, standardised tool-making sustained for over a million years.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;British Museum collection online (link out);Portable Antiquities Scheme (CC BY)
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society. Earliest dates from Kokiselei (Kenya).

name: Middle Stone Age
date_note: c. 300,000–30,000 years ago; regional end dates vary
making_significance: Early Homo sapiens made prepared-core points, ochre pigments and shell beads, the earliest evidence of symbolic adornment.
materials_techniques: prepared-core (Levallois) knapping; hafting with adhesives; ochre processing; shell perforation
object_types: points; blades; ochre pieces; shell beads
defined_by: A. J. H. Goodwin and C. van Riet Lowe (1929)
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society. Broad African period-industry; also used for Jebel Irhoud (Morocco, c. 300 ka).

name: Aterian
making_significance: North African MSA toolmakers made tanged points for hafting and some of the earliest shell beads.
defined_by: Named after Bir el-Ater (Algeria) by French prehistorians
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society.

name: Nubian Complex
date_note: c. 130,000–70,000 years ago in Nubia and Dhofar (Oman)
making_significance: A distinctive Levallois point method found in Nubia and in southern Arabia, used to trace early human movements out of Africa.
defined_by: Anthony Marks and Philip Van Peer; applied to Arabia by Jeffrey Rose et al. (2011)
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society. Arabian attribution debated.

name: Still Bay
making_significance: Southern African makers pressure-flaked bifacial points, sometimes heat-treating silcrete, alongside engraved ochre at Blombos Cave.
materials_techniques: heat treatment; pressure flaking; ochre engraving
object_types: bifacial points; engraved ochre; shell beads
defined_by: Named after Still Bay (South Africa); Goodwin and van Riet Lowe (1929)
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society.

name: Howiesons Poort
making_significance: Makers produced backed blades for composite tools and engraved ostrich eggshell water containers with repeated patterns.
materials_techniques: backed-blade production; composite hafting; eggshell engraving
defined_by: Named after Howiesons Poort shelter (South Africa)
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society.

name: Later Stone Age
date_note: from c. 50,000–40,000 years ago; forager toolkits persist into recent centuries
making_significance: Microlithic toolkits, ostrich-eggshell beads and rock art made by African foragers over tens of thousands of years.
materials_techniques: microlith production; bead making; rock painting
defined_by: A. J. H. Goodwin and C. van Riet Lowe (1929)
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society. Descendant forager communities (e.g. San) are living.

name: Iberomaurusian
making_significance: North African foragers made bladelet tools and buried their dead in large cemeteries, with evidence of tooth avulsion.
notes: Known largely from cemeteries (Taforalt, Afalou).

name: Capsian
making_significance: Capsian foragers of Tunisia and Algeria left snail-shell middens, engraved ostrich eggshell and decorated stones.
defined_by: Jacques de Morgan, after Gafsa (Latin Capsa)

name: Kiffian
making_significance: Early Holocene 'Green Sahara' fisher-hunters made bone harpoons and wavy-line pottery by now-dry lakes.
notes: Known mostly from the Gobero cemetery.

name: Faiyum A
making_significance: Early Egyptian farmers stored grain in basket-lined pits and made linen and pottery by Lake Qarun.

name: Badarian
making_significance: Upper Egyptian communities made thin rippled pottery, ivory combs and cosmetic palettes, known mostly from graves.
materials_techniques: rippled black-topped pottery; ivory carving; stone palettes
functions: food and storage;clothing and adornment;ritual and belief
defined_by: Guy Brunton and Gertrude Caton-Thompson, after el-Badari
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Naqada
making_significance: Predynastic Egyptian workshops made painted pottery, flint knives, stone vessels and ceremonial palettes before unification.
materials_techniques: ripple-flaked flint; stone-vessel drilling; painted pottery; copper
object_types: decorated pottery; palettes; knives; stone vessels
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;food and storage
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Khartoum Mesolithic
making_significance: Nile foragers made some of Africa's earliest pottery, decorated with wavy lines, and bone harpoons.
materials_techniques: early pottery (wavy-line, dotted wavy-line); bone working

name: A-Group
making_significance: Lower Nubian communities made eggshell-thin painted pottery and traded with Predynastic Egypt.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Known mainly from cemeteries; the 'A-Group' letter labels are Reisner's.

name: C-Group
making_significance: Lower Nubian cattle-herders made incised black pottery and stone grave superstructures.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Kerma
making_significance: Kerma potters made black-topped beakers of extraordinary thinness and the city had monumental mud-brick deffufa.
materials_techniques: black-topped fine pottery; mud-brick monumental building; faience; mica ornament
functions: food and storage;ritual and belief;rule and display
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Royal tumuli included human sacrifice; handle remains carefully.

name: X-Group
making_significance: Post-Meroitic rulers at Ballana and Qustul were buried with silver crowns, horse gear and imported goods.

name: D'mt / pre-Aksumite
making_significance: Highland Ethiopian and Eritrean communities built temples such as Yeha in South Arabian style.
notes: Degree of South Arabian migration vs local agency is debated.

name: Savanna Pastoral Neolithic
making_significance: East African herders made stone bowls and obsidian tools and moved cattle, sheep and goats across the Rift Valley.
notes: Many sites are burial cairns.

name: Urewe
making_significance: Early Iron Age Great Lakes communities smelted iron and made distinctive dimple-based pottery.
notes: Often linked to Bantu-speaking expansions; link language to material with care.

name: Triangular Incised Ware
making_significance: Early coastal pottery ancestral to Swahili towns, showing their African roots.
notes: Also called Tana tradition; ties to CIV Swahili.

name: Engaruka
making_significance: Farmers in northern Tanzania built stone-walled terraces and irrigation channels.

name: Tichitt tradition
making_significance: Agro-pastoralists built dry-stone walled villages along the Tichitt–Walata escarpments, among the earliest in West Africa.

name: Kintampo
making_significance: Early farming communities made grooved stone 'rasps' (possibly for pottery), clay figurines and ground-stone axes.

name: Nok
date_note: c. 1500 BCE–1 CE; terracottas from c. 900 BCE (Goethe University chronology)
making_significance: Farming communities in central Nigeria made large fired-clay figures and smelted iron.
materials_techniques: terracotta modelling and firing; iron smelting
object_types: terracotta figures; pottery; iron tools; grinding stones
defined_by: Bernard Fagg (1940s), after the village of Nok
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Existing in project. Terracottas heavily looted and faked; use only excavated or pre-1970 documented pieces.

name: Gajiganna
making_significance: Herders and later farmers settled the Lake Chad firki plains, making impressed pottery.

name: Sao
date_note: c. 6th century BCE to 16th century CE (dates debated)
making_significance: Communities south of Lake Chad made terracotta figures, bronze ornaments and large burial jars.
defined_by: Kotoko and Kanuri oral tradition; Jean-Paul Lebeuf's excavations (1930s–)
notes: 'Sao' is a name from oral tradition for earlier peoples; Kotoko communities claim descent.

name: Djenné-Djenno
making_significance: An early West African city without a citadel, with iron working, pottery and trade in the Inland Niger Delta.
materials_techniques: iron smelting; pottery; mud-brick; copper import
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)

name: Inland Niger Delta terracottas
making_significance: Makers in the Inland Niger Delta modelled seated and kneeling clay figures, later looted in large numbers.
notes: Mali restricted export (1970s); much looting; strict provenance. F1.24 case.

name: Bura
making_significance: A burial tradition with terracotta heads and figures set on funerary jars.

name: Igbo-Ukwu
making_significance: Makers cast highly detailed leaded-bronze vessels and ornaments using local ores and imported glass beads.
materials_techniques: lost-wax casting of leaded bronze; beadwork
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;clothing and adornment
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;British Museum collection online (link out)
notes: Includes a burial chamber and a shrine repository; Igbo living community.

name: Senegambian stone circles
making_significance: Communities quarried and set laterite pillars in over a thousand circles.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out);open-access excavation reports

name: Tellem
making_significance: Tellem people buried their dead in cliff caves with textiles, headrests and wooden figures.
notes: Earliest cotton textiles in West Africa; cave burials.

name: Sapi
making_significance: Sapi carvers made ivory salt cellars and horns for Portuguese buyers, and steatite figures (nomoli).
defined_by: European art history; 'Sapi' from Portuguese sources
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection online (link out)

name: Kisalian
making_significance: Cemeteries at Sanga and Katoto contain copper crosses (currency), ironwork and pottery, foreshadowing the Luba state.

name: Lydenburg
making_significance: Early farmers in Mpumalanga made seven hollow terracotta heads, the earliest known in southern Africa.
defined_by: Found by Ludwig von Bezing (1957); archaeologists

name: Mapungubwe
making_significance: Early southern African class society with gold foil and imported glass beads.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Routes from CIV Mapungubwe; reburied remains.

name: Zimbabwe tradition
making_significance: Dry-stone walled centres across Zimbabwe, Botswana and Mozambique, including Great Zimbabwe and Khami.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Routes from CIV Great Zimbabwe.

name: Bokoni
making_significance: Farming communities built stone-walled homesteads, terraces and roads over a large landscape.

name: Dembeni phase
date_note: c. 9th–10th century CE (Mayotte and the Comoros)
making_significance: Early Comorian villages worked and traded chlorite-schist vessels, local pottery and imported Near Eastern and Chinese ceramics, linking Madagascar to the Swahili coast.
materials_techniques: chlorite-schist carving; pottery; shell bead making
functions: exchange and value;food and storage;clothing and adornment
notes: Named after the Dembeni site on Mayotte.

name: Mahilaka
making_significance: A walled port town where makers worked chlorite-schist, iron and glass beads for Indian Ocean trade.
materials_techniques: chlorite-schist carving; iron smelting; coral and stone building
notes: Site-based grouping; Malagasy and Swahili links.

name: Rasikajy
making_significance: Islamised trading communities buried their dead with Chinese celadon, glass, chlorite-schist vessels and iron, showing Madagascar's place in Indian Ocean exchange.
defined_by: French colonial excavators (early 20th c.); Pierre Vérin
notes: Known almost entirely from cemeteries; many grave goods removed in colonial period.

name: Mousterian
making_significance: Neanderthals (and in the Levant also Homo sapiens) made prepared-core flake tools, hafted with birch-tar and bitumen adhesives.
materials_techniques: Levallois knapping; adhesive making (birch tar, bitumen)
defined_by: Gabriel de Mortillet, after Le Moustier (France)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Portable Antiquities Scheme (CC BY);Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Stone-tool industry, not a people or society.

name: Natufian
making_significance: Sedentary foragers built round houses, carved bone and stone, used sickles on wild cereals and made bead headdresses.
materials_techniques: ground stone; bone carving; dentalium shell beadwork; sickle blades
functions: food and storage;clothing and adornment;shelter;ritual and belief
notes: Burials include adorned individuals; handle remains carefully.

name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A
making_significance: Early cultivators built round houses, the Jericho tower and storage buildings.
materials_techniques: stone architecture; ground stone; early cultivation

name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic B
making_significance: Farming villages made lime plaster, plastered skulls and large statues, and traded obsidian.
materials_techniques: lime plaster; naviform blade cores; obsidian exchange
object_types: plastered skulls; plaster statues ('Ain Ghazal); blades
notes: Plastered skulls are human remains: default-exclude from display.

name: Taş Tepeler
making_significance: Hunter-gatherer and early farming communities carved T-shaped pillars and animal reliefs in communal buildings.
defined_by: Şanlıurfa Neolithic research project (2020s); Klaus Schmidt (Göbekli Tepe, 1995 on)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out);open-access excavation reports
notes: Name is a recent regional grouping; Göbekli Tepe itself is PPNA/PPNB.

name: Central Anatolian Neolithic (Çatalhöyük)
making_significance: Densely packed houses with wall paintings, plaster reliefs, figurines and obsidian mirrors.
materials_techniques: mud-brick; wall painting; obsidian polishing; clay figurines
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Open Context (CC BY);UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Open Context holds Çatalhöyük data. Mellaart's later drawings include fabrications; flag.

name: Halaf
making_significance: Makers of finely painted polychrome pottery and stamp seals across northern Mesopotamia.
functions: food and storage;record and writing;ritual and belief
defined_by: Max von Oppenheim, after Tell Halaf
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Ubaid
making_significance: Ubaid communities made painted pottery, clay sickles and temples; their pottery reached the Gulf.
defined_by: Named after Tell al-'Ubaid (H. R. Hall and Leonard Woolley, 1919–)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Uruk
making_significance: Uruk workshops mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls and developed cylinder seals and proto-cuneiform.
materials_techniques: mould-made pottery; cylinder seals; accounting tokens
functions: record and writing;food and storage;rule and display
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Ghassulian
making_significance: Chalcolithic Levantine makers cast arsenical copper by lost-wax process (Nahal Mishmar hoard) and painted wall frescoes.
materials_techniques: lost-wax copper casting; ivory carving; wall painting

name: Proto-Elamite
making_significance: Proto-Elamite tablets and seals show an administrative writing system across the Iranian plateau.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Marlik
making_significance: A cemetery of elite tombs with repoussé gold and silver beakers, bronze weapons and zoomorphic pottery.
materials_techniques: gold and silver repoussé; bronze casting; burnished pottery
notes: Known almost entirely from tombs; 'Amlash' market pieces are often looted or fake.

name: Luristan bronzes
making_significance: Metalworkers of the Zagros cast bronze horse-bits, finials and weapons with animal imagery.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Most on the market were looted from graves from the 1920s; many fakes. F1.24 case.

name: Arabian Neolithic
making_significance: Herders and fishers across Arabia made fine bifacial arrowheads, shell ornaments and stone structures.
notes: Broad regional label; many local variants.

name: Hafit
making_significance: Early Bronze Age communities in the UAE and Oman built beehive stone tombs on ridges and imported Jemdet Nasr pottery.
materials_techniques: dry-stone tomb building; pottery import; copper
defined_by: Danish expedition (1959) at Jebel Hafit; later Emirati and Omani archaeology
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Part of the Al Ain UNESCO site (2011).

name: Umm an-Nar
making_significance: Umm an-Nar communities smelted copper, built stone towers and communal round tombs, and traded with Mesopotamia and the Indus.
materials_techniques: copper smelting; ashlar stone tombs; soft-stone vessels; date cultivation
object_types: circular tombs; towers; soft-stone vessels; copper ingots
functions: exchange and value;ritual and belief;food and storage;tools
defined_by: Danish expedition (P. V. Glob, 1959), after Umm an-Nar island (Abu Dhabi)
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Archaeological correlate of 'Magan'.

name: Wadi Suq
making_significance: Middle Bronze Age Oman peninsula communities with long collective tombs and new soft-stone vessel styles.

name: Dadanite–Lihyanite
making_significance: Oasis kingdoms at al-'Ula carved colossal statues and inscriptions in Dadanitic script.
functions: rule and display;record and writing;ritual and belief
notes: Chronology debated.

name: Shulaveri–Shomu
making_significance: Early farmers in Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan built round mud-brick houses; early grape wine residues come from their pots.

name: Maykop
making_significance: North Caucasus kurgan burials with gold and silver vessels and bulls, and early arsenical bronze.
materials_techniques: gold and silver working; arsenical bronze; kurgans
defined_by: Nikolai Veselovsky (1897), after the Maykop kurgan

name: Kura–Araxes
making_significance: Makers of hand-burnished black-and-red pottery and hearths spread from the Caucasus to the Levant.
notes: Levantine variant called Khirbet Kerak ware.

name: Trialeti
making_significance: Middle Bronze Age kurgans in Georgia with gold goblets and silver vessels.

name: Colchian
date_note: c. 1700–600 BCE (western Georgia); later Colchis continues into Classical period
making_significance: Western Georgian smiths cast bronze axes, hoes and figurines and worked early iron; the region's gold fed the Greek Golden Fleece story.
materials_techniques: bronze casting; iron working; gold working
notes: Distinguish Bronze Age Colchian culture from Classical-era Colchis (Vani).

name: Koban
making_significance: North Caucasus smiths made engraved bronze axes and belt buckles.
defined_by: Rudolf Virchow and others, after Koban (North Ossetia)

name: Aurignacian
making_significance: Early Homo sapiens in Europe made blade tools, carved ivory figurines, bone flutes and painted Chauvet Cave.
materials_techniques: blade knapping; ivory carving; bone-flute making; cave painting
functions: tools;ritual and belief;play and music;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Henri Breuil and Émile Cartailhac (early 1900s), after Aurignac (France)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Stone-tool industry (with associated art), not a people.

name: Gravettian
making_significance: Gravettian makers fired clay figurines (Dolní Věstonice), carved 'Venus' figures and built mammoth-bone dwellings.
materials_techniques: fired clay; ivory and stone carving; mammoth-bone construction; textile impressions
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Stone-tool industry (with associated art), not a people. Earliest known fired-clay objects.

name: Solutrean
making_significance: Solutrean knappers made thin leaf-shaped points by pressure flaking and heat treatment.
notes: Stone-tool industry (with associated art), not a people. 'Solutrean hypothesis' for American origins is rejected.

name: Magdalenian
making_significance: Magdalenian makers carved spear-throwers and harpoons in antler and painted Lascaux and Altamira.
materials_techniques: antler carving; cave painting and engraving; eyed-needle sewing
object_types: spear-throwers; harpoons; engraved plaques; cave art
defined_by: Gabriel de Mortillet, after La Madeleine (France)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Stone-tool industry (with associated art), not a people.

name: Maglemosian
making_significance: Mesolithic foragers of the North European Plain made bone and antler harpoons, amber carvings and dugout canoes.
materials_techniques: bone and antler working; amber carving; dugout canoe making
free_sources: National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Ertebølle
making_significance: Coastal foragers of southern Scandinavia made pottery, paddles and shell middens before adopting farming.
materials_techniques: pointed-base pottery; wooden paddles; fish traps
free_sources: National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Lepenski Vir
making_significance: Danube Gorges foragers built trapezoidal houses and carved sandstone boulder sculptures with fish-like faces.

name: Starčevo–Körös–Criș
making_significance: Early farming communities of the Balkans and Carpathian Basin made pottery and figurines.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Europeana (filter by rights)

name: Cardial Ware
making_significance: Early Mediterranean farmers decorated pots with cockle-shell (Cardium) impressions as farming spread by sea.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Europeana (filter by rights)

name: Linear Pottery
making_significance: First farmers of central Europe built timber longhouses and made band-decorated pottery.
materials_techniques: timber longhouse construction; pottery; polished stone adzes
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Europeana (filter by rights)

name: Vinča
making_significance: Vinča communities in the central Balkans made abundant clay figurines and some of the earliest copper smelting in Europe.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Existing in project. 'Vinča symbols' are not proven writing.

name: Varna culture
making_significance: The Varna cemetery holds the world's oldest large assemblage of worked gold, alongside copper and Spondylus shell.
materials_techniques: gold working; copper; Spondylus shell working
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment

name: Cucuteni–Trypillia
making_significance: Makers of painted spiral pottery who built very large settlements (mega-sites) in Ukraine and Moldova.
defined_by: Named after Cucuteni (Romania, 1884) and Trypillia (Ukraine; Vikentiy Khvoyka, 1890s)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Ukrainian heritage at risk from war.

name: Funnelbeaker
making_significance: Northern European farmers built megalithic tombs and made funnel-necked pottery and flint axes.
free_sources: National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA);Swedish History Museum (CC BY);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights)

name: Maltese Temple culture
making_significance: Maltese communities built megalithic temples and the Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum with carved figures.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)

name: Grooved Ware
making_significance: British Neolithic flat-based pottery linked to henges and Orkney settlements like Skara Brae.

name: Comb Ceramic
making_significance: Forager potters of northeastern Europe decorated pots with comb impressions and carved elk-head figures.
free_sources: Finna / Finnish Heritage Agency (CC BY);Wikimedia Commons

name: Yamnaya
making_significance: Pontic–Caspian steppe herders used wagons and built kurgans; ancient DNA links them to later European populations.
materials_techniques: wagon building; kurgan construction; copper working
notes: Ancient DNA has made the name a proxy for 'Indo-European' migration; treat carefully.

name: Corded Ware
making_significance: Makers of cord-impressed beakers and stone battle axes, known largely from single graves.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights);National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA)

name: Únětice
making_significance: Central European Early Bronze Age metalworkers who made ingot torcs, daggers and the Nebra sky disc.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
defined_by: Čeněk Rýzner (1879), after Únětice near Prague
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Europeana (filter by rights)

name: El Argar
making_significance: Southeastern Iberian hilltop towns with bronze and silver work and burials under houses.

name: Nordic Bronze Age
making_significance: Scandinavian bronze-casters made lurs, the Trundholm sun chariot and oak-coffin burials with preserved textiles.
materials_techniques: bronze casting; wool textiles; rock carving
functions: ritual and belief;play and music;clothing and adornment
free_sources: National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA);Swedish History Museum (CC BY);Wikimedia Commons

name: Urnfield
making_significance: Central European communities cremated their dead and made sheet-bronze vessels and armour.

name: Villanovan
date_note: c. 900–700 BCE (earliest Iron Age phase of Etruria and parts of northern Italy)
making_significance: Villanovan communities cremated their dead in biconical and hut-shaped urns and made bronze helmets and fibulae, forerunners of Etruscan crafts.
materials_techniques: bronze sheet work; impasto pottery; cremation
object_types: hut urns; biconical urns; crested helmets; fibulae
defined_by: Giovanni Gozzadini (1850s), after Villanova near Bologna
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Routes to CIV Etruscan.

name: Hallstatt
date_note: Hallstatt C–D c. 800–450 BCE (Hallstatt A–B overlap the Urnfield period)
making_significance: Salt miners and elite households in central Europe used iron, imported Greek and Etruscan vessels and made patterned wool twills, preserved in the Hallstatt salt mines.
materials_techniques: salt mining; iron smithing; twill weaving; sheet-bronze
functions: rule and display;clothing and adornment;exchange and value;ritual and belief
defined_by: Named after Hallstatt (Austria; cemetery excavated from 1846 by Johann Georg Ramsauer); Hallstatt/La Tène division by Hans Hildebrand (1870s)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights);open-access excavation reports
notes: Routes from CIV Celtic.

name: La Tène
date_note: c. 450 BCE to Roman conquest (1st century BCE); later in Ireland
making_significance: Iron Age metalworkers made curvilinear ornament on torcs, scabbards, shields and mirrors that became the basis of 'Celtic art'.
materials_techniques: repoussé; enamel; iron smithing; wheel-thrown pottery
functions: clothing and adornment;war;rule and display;exchange and value
defined_by: Named after La Tène (Lake Neuchâtel, Switzerland; finds from 1857)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Portable Antiquities Scheme (CC BY);British Museum collection online (link out);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Routes from CIV Celtic.

name: Talaiotic
date_note: c. 1000 BCE to Roman conquest of the Balearics (123 BCE)
making_significance: Balearic islanders built cyclopean stone towers (talaiots) and T-shaped taula sanctuaries.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Menorca Talayotic sites UNESCO (2023).

name: Castro culture
date_note: c. 9th century BCE to Romanisation (1st century CE)
making_significance: Hillfort communities of northwest Iberia built round stone houses and made gold torcs and carved stone warriors.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights);open-access excavation reports

name: Djeitun
making_significance: The earliest farming villages of Central Asia, with mud-brick houses and painted pottery.

name: Botai
making_significance: Botai settlements hold early evidence of horse use, including possible bit wear and mare's-milk residues in pots.
notes: Botai horses were ancestors of Przewalski's horses, not modern domestic horses (aDNA, 2018).

name: Afanasievo
making_significance: Early herders of the Altai and Minusinsk basin with copper objects and kurgan burials, genetically related to Yamnaya.

name: Okunevo
making_significance: Okunevo communities carved stone stelae with faces and rayed designs.

name: Sintashta
making_significance: Fortified settlements with bronze metallurgy, where some of the earliest spoked-wheel chariots were buried.

name: Andronovo
making_significance: Bronze Age herders across the Kazakh steppe with timber houses, tin-bronze and geometric pottery.
notes: Often called a horizon or 'community' of related cultures (Alakul, Fedorovo).

name: Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex
making_significance: Walled oasis towns (Gonur Depe) with compartmented seals, composite stone figures and metalwork.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Routes from CIV Oxus; many 'Bactrian' objects on the market are looted or fake.

name: Saka
making_significance: Saka metalworkers in Kazakhstan and the Tian Shan made gold 'animal style' ornaments, including the Issyk 'Golden Man' costume.
functions: clothing and adornment;rule and display;ritual and belief
notes: Closely related to Scythians; routes from CIV Scythian.

name: Xiaohe
making_significance: Desert burials preserved felt, woven wool, baskets and early kefir cheese.
functions: clothing and adornment;food and storage;ritual and belief
notes: Preserved human bodies; default-exclude. Politically sensitive in Xinjiang.

name: Deer stone–khirigsuur complex
making_significance: Late Bronze Age herders carved deer stones and built large stone mounds (khirigsuurs) with horse offerings.

name: Pazyryk
making_significance: Frozen Altai tombs preserved felt hangings, a knotted pile carpet, tattooed skin, saddles and wooden carvings.
materials_techniques: felt appliqué; pile-carpet knotting; wood carving; tattooing
object_types: Pazyryk carpet; felt hangings; saddles; headdresses
functions: clothing and adornment;ritual and belief;transport;rule and display
notes: Altai communities protest the removal of the Ukok 'princess' (1993); oldest known pile carpet (Hermitage).

name: Tagar
making_significance: Iron Age herders of southern Siberia cast bronze animal-style knives and built large kurgans.

name: Tashtyk
making_significance: Tashtyk communities of southern Siberia made painted plaster funerary masks and dolls holding cremated remains.
materials_techniques: plaster moulding and painting; textiles; wood carving

name: Xiongnu
date_note: c. 209 BCE–1st century CE (political confederation); archaeological culture to c. 2nd century
making_significance: Xiongnu elite tombs held Chinese silks, Greco-Bactrian textiles and steppe metalwork, showing a nomadic empire at the centre of exchange.
materials_techniques: gold and bronze belt plaques; felt; imported silk
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Chinese historical sources (Sima Qian); Mongolian and Russian archaeology (Noin-Ula, 1924)

name: Mal'ta–Buret'
making_significance: Upper Palaeolithic hunters carved mammoth-ivory figurines and birds and built semi-subterranean houses.
notes: A Mal'ta child genome (2013) links Siberians and Native Americans.

name: Kitoi
making_significance: Hunter-gatherer cemeteries by Lake Baikal with fishing gear, ochre and nephrite rings.
materials_techniques: nephrite working; bone and antler tools

name: Okhotsk culture
making_significance: Maritime hunters of the Okhotsk Sea carved ivory and bone and kept bear-skull shrines in their houses.
materials_techniques: bone and ivory carving; sea-mammal hunting
notes: Links with later Ainu bear ritual debated.

name: Xinglongwa
making_significance: Planned villages of pit houses with some of the earliest carved jade (slit rings) in China.

name: Peiligang
making_significance: Early millet and rice farmers; the Jiahu site preserved bone flutes and early fermented-drink residues.
functions: food and storage;play and music;ritual and belief

name: Hemudu
making_significance: Waterlogged rice-farming villages with pile-built houses using mortise-and-tenon joinery and carved bone and ivory.
object_types: stilt houses; bone tools; lacquered bowl

name: Yangshao
making_significance: Millet-farming villages made red painted pottery, some with fish and human-face motifs.
defined_by: Johan Gunnar Andersson (1921), after Yangshao village
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Majiayao
making_significance: Potters made spiral-painted jars and one of the earliest bronze knives in China.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Dawenkou
making_significance: Burials with pottery, jade and ivory show growing social ranking; some pots bear early signs.
functions: food and storage;rule and display;ritual and belief

name: Hongshan
making_significance: Hongshan makers carved jade 'pig-dragons' and hooked cloud pendants and built stone cairns and a 'goddess temple' at Niuheliang.
materials_techniques: jade carving; stone cairn building; clay sculpture
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Jades are mostly from burials; many fakes on the market.

name: Liangzhu
making_significance: Liangzhu jade workers carved cong and bi with fine incised masks, and the city had walls and a large dam system.
materials_techniques: jade carving with abrasives; earth dam engineering; lacquer
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;food and storage
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)

name: Longshan
date_note: c. 3000–1900 BCE (lower and middle Yellow River)
making_significance: Longshan potters threw eggshell-thin black cups on a fast wheel; walled towns such as Taosi appear.
defined_by: Excavations at Chengziya (1930); Li Ji and others
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Distinct from HOR Longshan horizon (K. C. Chang).

name: Shimao
making_significance: A stone-walled city with carved stone reliefs and jades set into walls.
notes: Some human sacrifice at gates; care with remains.

name: Erlitou
making_significance: Erlitou foundries made the first piece-mould cast bronze vessels in China; its palace complex is linked by some to the Xia.
notes: Xia identification is debated.

name: Erligang
making_significance: Early Shang bronze workshops spread standardised vessels across a broad region.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Sanxingdui
date_note: c. 1700–1150 BCE; sacrificial pits c. 1200–1100 BCE
making_significance: Sichuan bronze-casters made large masks, a bronze tree and a standing figure unlike Shang work.
notes: Sacrificial pits (objects deliberately buried).

name: Jinsha
making_significance: Successor centre to Sanxingdui whose makers cut the gold 'sun and immortal birds' foil disc and worked ivory, jade and bronze.
materials_techniques: gold foil cutting; jade carving; ivory; bronze casting
object_types: gold sun-bird disc; jade cong; ivory tusks; bronze figures
notes: Sun-bird motif is China's official cultural heritage logo.

name: Dian
date_note: c. 4th century BCE–1st century CE (Lake Dian, Yunnan)
making_significance: Dian bronze-casters made cowrie containers topped with miniature scenes of weaving, ritual and warfare, and bronze drums.
materials_techniques: lost-wax and piece-mould bronze casting; gilding
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value;clothing and adornment
notes: Scenes show women weaving on backstrap looms (F1.18).

name: Chulmun
making_significance: Korean Neolithic foragers and early cultivators made comb-pattern pottery.
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons

name: Mumun
making_significance: Rice-farming villages made undecorated pottery, polished red jars and stone daggers, and began bronze use.
materials_techniques: plain and red-burnished pottery; polished stone daggers; bronze (later)
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Korean dolmen tradition
making_significance: Communities raised thousands of stone dolmens, the densest concentration in the world.
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)

name: Jōmon
date_note: c. 14,000–300 BCE; end dates vary regionally (Yayoi began earlier in Kyushu)
making_significance: Jōmon foragers made some of the world's earliest pottery, cord-marked and later flame-rimmed, plus lacquer and clay dogū figures.
materials_techniques: cord-marked pottery; lacquer; clay figurine making
functions: food and storage;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);ColBase, Japan NICH (check per-image terms);Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Northern Jōmon sites UNESCO (2021). Ainu are living descendants in the north.

name: Yayoi
date_note: c. 900 BCE–250 CE (AMS revision of older c. 300 BCE start)
making_significance: Wet-rice farmers, arriving from the Korean peninsula and mixing with Jōmon people, made bronze bells (dōtaku) and wheel-finished pottery.
materials_techniques: paddy rice farming; bronze casting; iron; weaving
functions: food and storage;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);ColBase, Japan NICH (check per-image terms);Wikimedia Commons

name: Kofun
making_significance: Elite keyhole-shaped tombs were ringed by clay haniwa figures of people, horses and houses.
materials_techniques: tomb building; haniwa terracotta; Sue stoneware
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);ColBase, Japan NICH (check per-image terms);Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Imperial tombs are sacred and closed to excavation (Imperial Household Agency).

name: Satsumon
making_significance: Hokkaido communities made scratched-pattern pottery and are considered ancestral to Ainu culture.
free_sources: ColBase, Japan NICH (check per-image terms);open-access excavation reports
notes: Ainu are a living Indigenous people, recognised 2019.

name: Mehrgarh (Neolithic)
making_significance: One of South Asia's earliest farming villages, with mud-brick storage, early cotton and the earliest known drilled teeth.
functions: food and storage;clothing and adornment;shelter;care and access

name: Early Harappan
making_significance: Walled towns with painted pottery before the integration of the Mature Harappan phase.
notes: Member of CIV Indus Valley.

name: Mature Harappan
making_significance: Planned brick cities (Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira) with seals, weights and long-drilled carnelian beads.
materials_techniques: fired brick; carnelian drilling; steatite seals; faience
functions: record and writing;exchange and value;clothing and adornment;shelter
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Member of CIV Indus Valley.

name: Late Harappan
making_significance: Regional successor phases (e.g. Jhukar, Rangpur, Cemetery H) in which large cities shrank but bead-making, pottery and farming continued and shifted east and south.
notes: Member of CIV Indus Valley; avoid 'collapse' framing.

name: Ochre Coloured Pottery
making_significance: Upper Ganges communities made ochre-washed pottery and are associated with copper hoards; burials at Sinauli held wooden carts sheathed in copper.
materials_techniques: ochre-slipped pottery; copper casting; copper sheathing
object_types: pottery; copper harpoons; anthropomorphic figures; carts
defined_by: B. B. Lal (1950s) and later Archaeological Survey of India (Sinauli, 2018)
notes: Sinauli 'chariot' interpretation debated.

name: Painted Grey Ware
making_significance: Iron Age farming communities made fine wheel-thrown grey pottery painted in black and began iron working in the Ganga plain.
materials_techniques: fine grey pottery; iron smithing; glass beads
notes: Often linked to later Vedic texts and Mahabharata sites; that link is contested.

name: Northern Black Polished Ware
making_significance: A glossy, metallic-looking black pottery used in the early historic cities of the Ganga plain, including under the Mauryas.
functions: food and storage;rule and display;exchange and value
notes: Luxury ware; linked with second urbanisation.

name: Deccan Chalcolithic
making_significance: Farming villages of the Deccan made painted pottery and copper tools; Inamgaon and Daimabad yielded bronze sculptures (date debated).
object_types: painted pottery; urn burials; copper axes
defined_by: H. D. Sankalia and Deccan College (1950s–80s)
notes: Groups several named cultures; Daimabad bronzes' date contested.

name: Southern Neolithic
making_significance: Herders and farmers of the southern Deccan burned cattle dung into large ash mounds and made ground-stone axes and rock art.
materials_techniques: ground stone; dung burning; rock painting and bruising

name: Megalithic South India
other_names: Iron Age South India; megalithic burials
making_significance: Iron Age communities built stone-circle and cist burials with black-and-red ware, iron tools and carnelian beads.
materials_techniques: iron smithing; black-and-red ware; bead drilling; stone setting
notes: Includes Adichanallur urn cemetery.

name: Gandhara Grave culture
making_significance: Cemeteries in the Swat valley with grey pottery and copper, linked by genetics to later South Asian populations.
defined_by: Italian Archaeological Mission (IsMEO) and Ahmad Hasan Dani (1960s)

name: Balangoda culture
date_note: from c. 38,000 years ago (Batadomba-lena, Fa-Hien) to the Holocene
making_significance: Sri Lankan rainforest foragers made geometric microliths and bone tools at a very early date.
notes: Stone-tool industry. Vedda people are a living community.

name: Burzahom (Kashmir Neolithic)
making_significance: Kashmir valley farmers dug pit houses, made harvesting knives and bone tools, and carved a hunting scene on stone.
materials_techniques: pit-dwelling construction; bone tools; ground-stone knives

name: Karuo
making_significance: Early farming villages of eastern Tibet with millet, stone houses, painted pottery and shell ornaments.
materials_techniques: stone house building; pottery; ground stone

name: Qugong
date_note: early phase at the type site re-dated to c. 1400–1300 cal BCE by 2024 re-excavation (earlier estimates c. 2000–1500 or 1750–1100 BCE); end approximate (Lhasa)
making_significance: A Neolithic settlement near Lhasa whose potters made polished, incised and stamped round-based wares.
materials_techniques: burnished pottery; incised and stamped decoration
notes: Copper/metal claim removed: not reported in the 2024 re-excavation (Neolithic assemblage); restore only with a source.

name: Mustang cave tombs
making_significance: Cliff-cut cave burials with wooden coffins, a gold-and-silver funerary mask, textiles and beads.
materials_techniques: wood coffin making; gold and silver repoussé; weaving

name: Hoabinhian
making_significance: Forager toolkit of unifacially flaked cobbles (sumatraliths) used across mainland Southeast Asia and Sumatra.
defined_by: Madeleine Colani (1920s), after Hòa Bình province (Vietnam)
notes: Stone-tool industry.

name: Phùng Nguyên
making_significance: Neolithic to early Bronze Age villages with incised pottery and jade.

name: Ban Chiang
date_note: c. 2100 BCE–200 CE; start of bronze working debated (c. 1500–1000 BCE)
making_significance: Northeast Thai villagers buried their dead with red-on-buff painted pottery, bronze bracelets and later iron, a key case for independent Southeast Asian metallurgy.
functions: ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;food and storage
defined_by: Found 1966; Thai Fine Arts Department and University of Pennsylvania (Chester Gorman, Pisit Charoenwongsa)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out);open-access excavation reports
notes: Heavily looted in the 1960s–70s; US federal investigation (2008) led to returns to Thailand. F1.24 case.

name: Đông Sơn
date_note: c. 1000 BCE–1st century CE (Red River valley), drums traded later
making_significance: Đông Sơn bronze-casters made large decorated kettle drums that were carried across Island Southeast Asia.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;play and music;exchange and value
defined_by: After Đông Sơn village (Thanh Hóa), excavated 1924–; EFEO (Victor Goloubew)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Drums reach Indonesia (Heger type I).

name: Sa Huỳnh
date_note: c. 1000 BCE–200 CE (central and southern Vietnam)
making_significance: Coastal communities buried their dead in large jars with nephrite lingling-o earrings and glass and carnelian beads.
materials_techniques: jar burial; nephrite and glass bead working; iron
functions: ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;exchange and value
notes: Taiwanese nephrite in Sa Huỳnh ornaments shows long-distance exchange.

name: Plain of Jars
date_note: c. 500 BCE–500 CE (dates debated; some jars placed earlier)
making_significance: Communities in Laos quarried and set over two thousand stone jars used in mortuary ritual.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out);open-access excavation reports
notes: Unexploded ordnance from the 1964–73 bombing still at sites (F1.19a).

name: Óc Eo
making_significance: A canal-linked port where makers worked gold, glass beads and tin, trading with India, China and Rome.
materials_techniques: gold working; glass bead making; canal engineering
object_types: beads; seals; gold plaques; Roman coins
notes: Links to the Chinese-recorded polity 'Funan'.

name: Dvaravati
making_significance: Mon-speaking Buddhist communities made stucco and terracotta sculpture, dharmachakra wheels and moated towns.
defined_by: Art historians and archaeologists (from coins inscribed 'Dvaravati')
notes: Art-historical as much as archaeological grouping.

name: Dapenkeng
making_significance: Earliest Neolithic of Taiwan with cord-marked pottery, often linked to the beginnings of Austronesian dispersal.
materials_techniques: cord-marked pottery; ground stone; bark-cloth beaters
notes: Taiwanese Indigenous peoples are living descendants.

name: Beinan
date_note: c. 3300–300 BCE (east Taiwan; main phase c. 1500–800 BCE)
making_significance: A large slate-slab settlement and cemetery with nephrite earrings (including lingling-o and human-animal jades).

name: Toalean
making_significance: Sulawesi foragers made small serrated 'Maros points' and backed microliths.
notes: Stone-tool industry; a Toalean genome published 2021.

name: Arctic Small Tool tradition
making_significance: Palaeo-Inuit (Palaeo-Eskimo) peoples spread from Alaska to Greenland with finely made microblades, burins and bow technology.
materials_techniques: microblade and burin production; bow and arrow
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA);open-access excavation reports
notes: 'Palaeo-Eskimo' is being replaced by 'Palaeo-Inuit' in some usage; check preferred term.

name: Saqqaq
making_significance: Early Greenlanders made stone and bone tools and sewn skin clothing; a Saqqaq hair sample gave the first ancient human genome (2010).
materials_techniques: stone knapping; bone and wood working; skin sewing
free_sources: National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA);open-access excavation reports

name: Dorset
making_significance: Dorset carvers made small ivory, antler and wood figures of bears, people and masks.
materials_techniques: ivory and antler carving; soapstone lamps; snow knife
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Inuit oral histories name them Tuniit.

name: Old Bering Sea
making_significance: Maritime hunters carved walrus-ivory harpoon parts and 'winged objects' with curvilinear engraving.
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Ivories mined from sites for the market; St Lawrence Island context.

name: Ipiutak
making_significance: A large settlement and cemetery with elaborate ivory carvings, openwork and inset eyes placed with the dead.
materials_techniques: ivory carving; openwork; jet and ivory inlay
defined_by: Helge Larsen, Froelich Rainey and Louis Giddings (1939–41)

name: Thule
date_note: c. 1000–1600 CE (spread from Alaska to Greenland c. 1200–1300)
making_significance: Ancestors of the Inuit spread across the Arctic with whale-bone houses, umiaks, dog sleds and toggling harpoons.
materials_techniques: whalebone construction; skin boat building; sled making; ivory carving
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Living Inuit communities; Inuit-led interpretation preferred.

name: Marpole
date_note: c. 500 BCE–500 CE (Fraser delta, Salish Sea)
making_significance: Coast Salish ancestral communities carved stone bowls, antler and wood and built plank houses.
materials_techniques: stone bowl carving; antler carving; plank house construction
notes: Marpole village site (c̓əsnaʔəm) is a Musqueam sacred place.

name: Locarno Beach
making_significance: Ancestral Coast Salish communities made ground-slate knives, labrets and carved antler before the Marpole phase.
materials_techniques: ground-slate working; antler carving; labret making
defined_by: Charles Borden (1950s), after Locarno Beach, Vancouver

name: Clovis
making_significance: Clovis knappers made fluted spear points traded over long distances across North America.
defined_by: Named after Clovis, New Mexico (Blackwater Draw, 1930s)
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Stone-tool tradition; 'Clovis first' has been disproven.

name: Western Stemmed Tradition
date_note: c. 14,000–10,000 BP; some dates as early as 16,000 BP (Cooper's Ferry)
making_significance: Stemmed points in the Great Basin and Plateau, possibly as old as or older than Clovis.
notes: Stone-tool tradition.

name: Hohokam
making_significance: Hohokam farmers dug hundreds of kilometres of irrigation canals, made red-on-buff pottery, ball courts and acid-etched shell.
materials_techniques: canal engineering; red-on-buff pottery; shell etching
object_types: canals; pottery; etched shell; ball courts
functions: food and storage;clothing and adornment;play and music
defined_by: Harold Gladwin and Emil Haury (1930s); term from O'odham
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: O'odham peoples are descendants; the name's translation is debated.

name: Mogollon
making_significance: Mogollon villagers built pit houses and later pueblos and made brown and painted pottery.

name: Mimbres
making_significance: Mimbres potters painted black-on-white bowls with figures and patterns, many placed over faces in burials with a hole 'killed' through them.
notes: Bowls largely looted from graves; NAGPRA; display with care.

name: Ancestral Puebloan
date_note: Basketmaker II from c. 1500 BCE in some chronologies; Pueblo IV to c. 1600
making_significance: Builders of masonry great houses (Chaco) and cliff dwellings (Mesa Verde) who made coiled baskets, turkey-feather blankets and painted pottery.
materials_techniques: masonry; coiled basketry; black-on-white pottery; turkey-feather weaving
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Routes from CIV Ancestral Puebloan.

name: Casas Grandes
making_significance: Paquimé bred scarlet macaws, made polychrome effigy pottery and built multi-storey adobe compounds.
materials_techniques: adobe building; polychrome pottery; macaw breeding
object_types: effigy jars; macaw pens; shell ornaments
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)

name: Maritime Archaic
making_significance: Coastal hunters made ground-slate tools and buried their dead with red ochre (Port au Choix).
materials_techniques: ground slate; red ochre; bone carving

name: Old Copper complex
date_note: c. 4000–1000 BCE (earliest perhaps c. 7000 BCE) (western Great Lakes)
making_significance: Among the world's earliest metalworkers, cold-hammering and annealing native copper into tools.

name: Poverty Point
making_significance: Hunter-gatherers built monumental concentric earthen ridges and mounds and made baked clay cooking objects.
materials_techniques: earthwork; baked clay objects; stone bead making
object_types: ridges; mounds; clay cooking balls; beads
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out);open-access excavation reports

name: Adena
making_significance: Adena communities built burial mounds and carved stone tablets and pipes.
defined_by: After the Adena estate (Chillicothe, Ohio), excavated 1901

name: Hopewell
making_significance: Hopewell makers built geometric earthworks and made mica cut-outs, copper plates and platform pipes from far-traded materials.
materials_techniques: earthwork; mica cutting; copper hammering; pipe carving
object_types: platform pipes; mica hands; copper birds
functions: ritual and belief;exchange and value;rule and display
defined_by: Warren K. Moorehead (1891), after Mordecai Hopewell's farm
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: See HOR Hopewell Interaction Sphere; Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks UNESCO (2023).

name: Mississippian
making_significance: Towns (Cahokia, Moundville, Etowah) with platform mounds, engraved shell gorgets, copper plates and effigy pottery.
materials_techniques: earthwork; shell engraving; copper repoussé; shell-tempered pottery
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Routes from CIV Mississippian.

name: Olmec
date_note: c. 1600–400 BCE (San Lorenzo c. 1400–1000; La Venta c. 1000–400 BCE)
making_significance: Gulf Coast makers carved colossal basalt heads, jade figures and celts, and buried massive serpentine offerings.
materials_techniques: basalt carving and transport; jade and serpentine working; ceramic figurines
object_types: colossal heads; altars; jade masks; celts
defined_by: Marshall Saville and George Vaillant (1920s); Matthew Stirling (1938–46)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Yale University Art Gallery (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Routes from CIV Olmec; see HOR Olmec horizon.

name: Tlatilco
making_significance: A village cemetery with hundreds of burials holding hand-modelled 'pretty lady' figurines and Olmec-style vessels.

name: Monte Albán (Zapotec)
making_significance: The Zapotec hilltop capital with carved 'Danzantes' slabs, painted tombs and ceramic effigy urns.
materials_techniques: stone relief carving; tomb painting; ceramic urn modelling
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Routes from CIV Zapotec; Tomb 7's goldwork is later Mixtec reuse.

name: West Mexican shaft tomb tradition
making_significance: Hollow ceramic figures of people, dogs and village scenes were placed in deep shaft-and-chamber tombs.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);LACMA (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Almost all known from looted tombs; many fakes. F1.24 case.

name: Classic Veracruz
making_significance: Gulf Coast makers carved stone ballgame yokes, hachas and palmas and made smiling-face ceramic figures.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Gran Coclé
date_note: c. 200–1500 CE; Sitio Conte burials c. 700–1000
making_significance: Panamanian makers produced polychrome pottery and cast and hammered gold, found in chiefly burials.
materials_techniques: polychrome pottery; lost-wax gold casting; depletion gilding
object_types: polychrome plates; gold plaques; ear rods
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
free_sources: Penn Museum online collection (link out);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Diquís
making_significance: Communities carved hundreds of near-perfect stone spheres and cast gold ornaments.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: UNESCO (2014).

name: Tairona
date_note: c. 900–1600 CE (Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta)
making_significance: Tairona builders made stone terraces, paths and Ciudad Perdida, and goldsmiths cast tumbaga pendants.
notes: Kogi, Arhuaco, Wiwa and Kankuamo are living descendant peoples; Ciudad Perdida is sacred to them.

name: Quimbaya
date_note: Early Quimbaya c. 500 BCE–600 CE (Cauca valley)
making_significance: Goldsmiths cast tumbaga figures and vessels by lost-wax; the 'Quimbaya Treasure' is in Madrid.
notes: Colombia's Constitutional Court ordered restitution efforts (2017). F1.24 case.

name: San Agustín
making_significance: Makers carved hundreds of monumental stone guardian statues over burial mounds.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: UNESCO (1995).

name: La Tolita–Tumaco
making_significance: Metalworkers here sintered platinum with gold, centuries before Europe worked platinum; potters made moulded figurines.
materials_techniques: platinum sintering; gold working; mould-made ceramics
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment

name: Casimiroid
making_significance: Among the earliest known settlers of the Greater Antilles, making large flaked-stone blades and, later, ground-stone tools.
defined_by: Irving Rouse, after the Casimira site (Dominican Republic)

name: Saladoid
making_significance: Farmer-potters from the Orinoco settled the Antilles, making white-on-red pottery and carved stone and shell amulets.
materials_techniques: white-on-red pottery; stone and shell carving
functions: food and storage;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Ostionoid
making_significance: Successor pottery series to Saladoid, ancestral to Taíno material culture, with ball courts appearing.

name: Chicoid
making_significance: Taíno-period pottery and carving series with modelled heads and incised decoration.
defined_by: Irving Rouse, after Boca Chica (Dominican Republic)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Routes from CIV Taíno.

name: Lucayan
making_significance: Lucayan islanders made shell-tempered Palmetto pottery and carved wooden duhos, and were enslaved en masse after 1492.

name: Colono ware
making_significance: Low-fired, hand-built earthenware made by enslaved Africans and Native Americans in the colonial Americas, direct evidence of everyday making under slavery.
materials_techniques: hand-built low-fired pottery; open firing; burnishing
defined_by: Ivor Noël Hume (1962, 'Colono-Indian ware'); Leland Ferguson ('Uncommon Ground', 1992)
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);open-access excavation reports;Wikimedia Commons
notes: A ware category, not a people; African vs Native American authorship debated regionally; content note for slavery.

name: Chinchorro
date_note: c. 7000–1500 BCE (artificial mummification from c. 5000 BCE)
making_significance: Coastal fishers of the Atacama made the world's earliest known artificially mummified bodies, reshaping them with clay, reeds and paint.
materials_techniques: artificial mummification; reed and clay modelling; fishing gear
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Human remains: default-exclude images; describe only.

name: Valdivia
making_significance: Among the earliest pottery makers of the Americas, making stone and ceramic female figurines and U-shaped villages.

name: Cupisnique
making_significance: Potters made stirrup-spout vessels and goldsmiths hammered sheet gold with feline imagery, linked to Chavín.

name: Paracas
making_significance: Paracas weavers made embroidered mantles of camelid fibre wrapped around the dead in large bundles.
materials_techniques: stem-stitch embroidery; resin-painted pottery; cranial modification
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Art Institute of Chicago (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Textiles came from mummy bundles; many looted and exported.

name: Nasca
making_significance: Makers of polychrome slip-painted pottery, textiles and the geoglyphs on the Nazca pampa.
materials_techniques: polychrome slip painting; geoglyph clearing; puquio engineering
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Art Institute of Chicago (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Routes from CIV Nazca.

name: Moche
making_significance: North-coast potters and metalworkers made mould-made portrait vessels, fineline painted scenes and gilded copper regalia.
materials_techniques: mould-made ceramics; fineline painting; depletion gilding; adobe platforms
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Art Institute of Chicago (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Routes from CIV Moche.

name: Recuay
making_significance: Highland makers of kaolin pottery with modelled scenes and stone sculpture of warriors.
materials_techniques: kaolin pottery; negative (resist) painting; stone carving

name: Sicán
making_significance: Sicán metalworkers smelted arsenical bronze on an industrial scale and made gold masks and tumi knives for elite tombs.
materials_techniques: arsenical bronze smelting; gold sheet work
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value

name: Chachapoya
making_significance: Cloud-forest builders of Kuélap and cliff-set sarcophagi and mausolea.
materials_techniques: stone masonry with friezes; clay sarcophagi

name: Diaguita
making_significance: Diaguita potters painted bowls and jars with dense geometric designs, later adapting them under Inca rule; Diaguita people are recognised in Chile and Argentina today.
object_types: painted bowls; duck-shaped jars; metal pectorals
functions: food and storage;rule and display;ritual and belief
defined_by: Spanish colonial name; Chilean and Argentine archaeology

name: Monte Alegre Paleoindian
making_significance: Early Amazonian foragers painted rock art and made triangular points.

name: Upano
making_significance: Lidar revealed rectangular platform mounds, plazas and long straight roads linking settlements.
materials_techniques: earth platform building; road building; pottery

name: Marajoara
making_significance: Marajó potters made painted, excised and modelled funerary urns and ceramic pubic covers (tangas).
materials_techniques: excised and painted ceramics; mound building
defined_by: Brazilian and US archaeologists (Meggers, Evans, Roosevelt, Schaan)
notes: Routes from CIV Marajoara.

name: Santarém
date_note: c. 1000–1600 CE (confluence of Tapajós and Amazon)
making_significance: Potters made elaborate caryatid and neck vessels with modelled figures; muiraquitã green-stone frogs circulated.

name: Casarabe
making_significance: Settlements with platform mounds, causeways, canals and reservoirs.

name: Upper Xingu ancestral settlements
making_significance: Large ditched villages linked by roads, ancestral to present Xinguano peoples.
materials_techniques: ditch and bank earthworks; roads; terra preta
notes: Kuikuro collaboration; living descendants.

name: Acre geoglyphs
date_note: c. 1st–13th century CE; construction dates vary by site
making_significance: Communities in the western Amazon dug hundreds of geometric ditched enclosures (squares, circles) within managed bamboo forest, showing large-scale landscape making without clear-cutting.
defined_by: Brazilian archaeologists (Alceu Ranzi, Denise Schaan; Jennifer Watling et al., 2017)
notes: Revealed by deforestation for cattle ranching (F1.22).

name: Sambaqui
making_significance: Coastal fisher-gatherers built shell mounds tens of metres high as cemeteries and landmarks, and polished stone animal sculptures (zooliths).
materials_techniques: shell-mound construction; stone polishing; bone working
defined_by: Tupi-derived name ('mound of shells'); Brazilian archaeologists
notes: Lowland South America, outside Amazonia proper; code AM-AMZ used as nearest region. Many mounds destroyed for lime.

name: Tupiguarani tradition
date_note: c. 500–1600 CE (dates vary; earlier in Amazonia)
making_significance: Potters made red-and-black painted and corrugated vessels, including large burial urns, across eastern South America.
materials_techniques: painted and corrugated pottery; urn burial
notes: Linked (with care) to Tupi-Guarani-speaking peoples, who are living communities.

name: Australian Core Tool and Scraper tradition
date_note: from first occupation (c. 50,000+ years ago) to the mid-Holocene; loosely defined
making_significance: A broad label for early Australian stone toolkits of cores, scrapers and, in the north, some of the world's oldest ground-edge axes.
materials_techniques: core reduction; edge-grinding (northern Australia, c. 45,000+ years)
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;Museums Victoria Collections (CC BY / public domain)
notes: Stone-tool tradition; old taxonomic term now used loosely. Aboriginal custodians must be consulted.

name: Australian Small Tool tradition
date_note: c. 5000 years ago to the colonial period
making_significance: Mid-Holocene Aboriginal toolmakers produced small backed points, pirri points and adze slugs for hafted tools.
materials_techniques: backing; pressure flaking; hafting with resin
object_types: backed points; pirri points; tula adzes
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;Museums Victoria Collections (CC BY / public domain)
notes: Stone-tool tradition. Living knowledge holders. Verify who coined the term.

name: Gwion Gwion
date_note: c. 12,700–11,500 years ago from mud-wasp-nest dating (Finch et al. 2020); older claims made
making_significance: A rock-painting tradition of the Kimberley showing finely painted figures with tassels, sashes and headdresses.
defined_by: Ngarinyin and other Kimberley Traditional Owners (Gwion Gwion); pastoralist Joseph Bradshaw's name (1891)
notes: Rock-art tradition, not a society. Use 'Gwion Gwion'; images only if community-published.

name: Lapita
date_note: c. 1350–500 BCE (Bismarck Archipelago to Tonga and Samoa)
making_significance: Lapita potters made dentate-stamped pottery with face and geometric designs as their communities settled Remote Oceania for the first time.
materials_techniques: dentate-stamped pottery; obsidian exchange; shell adze and ornament making; outrigger voyaging
object_types: stamped pots; shell rings; obsidian flakes
functions: food and storage;ritual and belief;transport;exchange and value
defined_by: Named after site 13 at Lapita, New Caledonia (E. W. Gifford and R. Shutler, 1952)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Auckland Museum Collections Online (CC BY)
notes: Existing in project. Teouma (Vanuatu) cemetery: funerary.

name: Polynesian Plainware
making_significance: Undecorated pottery that followed Lapita in western Polynesia before pottery-making ceased.

name: Ancestral Polynesian culture
making_significance: A reconstructed culture in western Polynesia whose adzes, fishhooks and words for crafts are traced by archaeology and language.
notes: Partly reconstructed from comparative linguistics.

name: Archaic East Polynesian
date_note: c. 1000–1450 CE (Society Islands to Aotearoa, Hawaiʻi and Rapa Nui)
making_significance: Settlers of eastern Polynesia made tanged adzes, one-piece fishhooks and whale-tooth ornaments during the last great voyaging settlement.
materials_techniques: adze grinding; bone and shell fishhooks; whale-ivory carving
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked);Auckland Museum Collections Online (CC BY);open-access excavation reports
notes: Aotearoa's 'Archaic' phase once called 'Moa-hunter'.

name: Pre-Latte
making_significance: The earliest settlers of remote Micronesia made red-slipped pottery with lime-filled stamped designs.
materials_techniques: red-slipped and lime-infilled pottery; shell ornament
notes: The Marianas crossing (c. 1500 BCE) was among the longest early ocean voyages.

name: Latte
making_significance: CHamoru ancestors raised stone pillars and capstones (latte) as house foundations.
notes: Latte stone is a living CHamoru symbol; consult CHamoru organisations.

name: Nan Madol (Saudeleur)
making_significance: Builders stacked columnar basalt into nearly a hundred artificial islets for a ceremonial and royal centre.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: UNESCO (2016). Pohnpeian community consultation.

name: Early Horizon
date_note: c. 900–200 BCE in John Rowe's Ica-based scheme
making_significance: A period when Chavín-related imagery in stone, textile, ceramic and gold spread widely across the Andes.
materials_techniques: stone carving; painted textiles; gold sheet work; stirrup-spout ceramics
object_types: carved slabs; painted cloths; gold crowns
defined_by: John H. Rowe and Dorothy Menzel (1960s), Ica valley master sequence
notes: Rowe's horizons alternate with 'Intermediate Periods'; routes from CIV Chavín.

name: Middle Horizon
making_significance: A period when Wari and Tiwanaku imagery, tapestry and ceramics spread across much of the Andes.
materials_techniques: interlocking tapestry; polychrome ceramics; planned architecture
functions: rule and display;clothing and adornment;ritual and belief
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Art Institute of Chicago (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;PeriodO
notes: Existing in project. Members: CIV Wari, CIV Tiwanaku.

name: Late Horizon
date_note: c. 1476–1534 in the Ica valley (Inca conquest to Spanish invasion)
making_significance: The period of Inca imperial rule, when state tapestry, aryballos jars and road-building were imposed across the Andes.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;PeriodO
notes: Dates are Ica-specific; Inca expansion began earlier elsewhere.

name: Olmec horizon
other_names: Early Formative 'Olmec style' horizon; San Lorenzo horizon
making_significance: A period when Olmec-style motifs on ceramics, jade and figurines appear across Mesoamerica from Guerrero to El Salvador.
materials_techniques: carved and incised ceramics; jade working
defined_by: Mesoamericanists (Kent Flannery; Michael Coe) in the 'mother culture' vs 'sister cultures' debate
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;PeriodO
notes: Contested: shared style may reflect exchange rather than Olmec dominance.

name: Mixteca-Puebla horizon
making_significance: A shared Postclassic painting style on codices, polychrome ceramics and murals across Mesoamerica.
materials_techniques: codex painting; polychrome ceramics; mural painting
functions: record and writing;ritual and belief;exchange and value
defined_by: George Vaillant (1940s); later 'Postclassic International Style' (Robertson, Boone)

name: Hopewell Interaction Sphere
making_significance: A network through which obsidian, mica, copper, shells and shark teeth moved across eastern North America into Hopewell ritual objects.
materials_techniques: long-distance exchange; mica cutting; copper hammering
object_types: mica cut-outs; copper plates; obsidian bifaces
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: An interaction sphere rather than a horizon in the strict sense; also a candidate for the Networks family.

name: Mississippian Ideological Interaction Sphere
making_significance: A shared iconography on shell, copper and pottery (falcon dancers, forked eyes) across Mississippian towns.
defined_by: Antonio Waring and Preston Holder (1945, 'Southern Cult'); renamed SECC and MIIS
notes: Interaction sphere; iconography sacred to descendant nations.

name: Chaco regional system
making_significance: A network of great houses and roads centred on Chaco Canyon through which turquoise, macaws and cacao were exchanged.
object_types: great houses; roads; turquoise; cylinder jars
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Regional system rather than strict horizon; Pueblo nations are descendants.

name: Amazonian Polychrome Tradition
making_significance: A widespread Amazonian tradition of red-and-black-on-white painted pottery, including large burial urns.
defined_by: Donald Lathrap and later Amazonian archaeologists
notes: A pottery tradition spanning many groups; treat as horizon.

name: Uruk expansion
making_significance: Uruk-style colonies and bevelled-rim bowls appeared from Anatolia to Iran, carrying accounting and craft practices.
materials_techniques: mould-made pottery; cylinder seals; accounting tokens
notes: Colonial/world-system model debated.

name: Bell Beaker phenomenon
making_significance: A widespread package of bell-shaped beakers, copper daggers, archer's wrist-guards and V-perforated buttons across Europe and northwest Africa.
materials_techniques: pottery; copper and gold working; stone wrist-guards
free_sources: Portable Antiquities Scheme (CC BY);Archaeology Data Service (open reports);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Also an ARC in some schemes; ancient DNA shows different population histories in Iberia and Britain.

name: Longshan horizon
making_significance: A proposed horizon of shared ceramic forms and rising elite craft across regional Chinese Neolithic cultures.
notes: Framework, not a single culture; routes to ARC Longshan, Liangzhu, Dawenkou.

name: Lapita horizon
making_significance: Dentate-stamped Lapita pottery marks a rapid horizon of settlement across Near and Remote Oceania.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Auckland Museum Collections Online (CC BY)
notes: Same phenomenon as ARC Lapita (existing); keep as horizon view for F1.30 or merge.

name: Austronesian expansion
date_note: c. 3000 BCE (Taiwan) to c. 1250 CE (Aotearoa); Madagascar c. 500–900 CE
making_significance: The spread of Austronesian-speaking voyagers carrying outrigger canoes, barkcloth, pottery and crops from Taiwan to Madagascar and Rapa Nui.
materials_techniques: outrigger canoe building; barkcloth; pottery; tattooing
defined_by: Linguists and archaeologists (Robert Blust; Peter Bellwood's 'Out of Taiwan' model)
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;Wikimedia Commons;Auckland Museum Collections Online (CC BY);Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked)
notes: A language dispersal, not a culture or horizon strictly; the 'Out of Taiwan' model is debated.

name: Sa Huỳnh–Kalanay interaction sphere
making_significance: A proposed South China Sea network through which pottery styles and nephrite lingling-o ornaments circulated.
notes: Solheim's pottery-complex framing is contested; nephrite sourcing (Taiwan) supports exchange.

name: Bantu-speaking expansions
other_names: Bantu expansion; Early Iron Age dispersal
date_note: c. 2000 BCE–1000 CE (from the Cameroon–Nigeria borderlands)
making_significance: The spread of Bantu languages, farming, pottery traditions and iron working across central, eastern and southern Africa.
defined_by: Linguists (Joseph Greenberg; Malcolm Guthrie) and archaeologists (David Phillipson)
notes: Language, genes and pottery do not map one-to-one; avoid 'migration of a people' shorthand.

name: Scytho-Siberian horizon
making_significance: A shared package of 'animal style' ornament, weapons and horse gear across the Eurasian steppe from the Black Sea to Mongolia.
materials_techniques: bronze and gold casting; felt; horse equipment
notes: Includes Scythian, Saka, Pazyryk, Tagar, Arzhan.
